svg.title: The EIGRP composite metric: minimum bandwidth plus summed delay, and why one slow hop decides the whole path
svg.desc: The classic formula is shown as 256 times the quantity ten to the seventh divided by the minimum bandwidth in kilobits per second, plus the sum of delays divided by ten. Bandwidth is taken as a minimum along the path, while delay is summed, so a single slow hop caps the metric for the whole path. A worked example shows a four hop path of 100G, 100G, 100M and 100G; the total delay is small but the minimum bandwidth is 100 Mbps, so the path is scored as a 100 Mbps path and loses to a three hop all-1G path even though it is far faster in reality. Wide metrics are explained as a 64 bit extension with a larger scale factor, needed above 10 Gbps because the classic 32 bit metric saturates. A closing note gives the design consequence: in a mixed bandwidth network the composite metric is dominated by the slowest link, so traffic engineering needs delay tuning or explicit policy rather than bandwidth.
svg.text: EIGRP metric = minimum bandwidth plus summed delay, scaled by 256
One term takes the minimum and the other adds — that asymmetry is the whole behaviour of the protocol
THE CLASSIC FORMULA
metric = 256 × [ ( 10⁷ / min bandwidth (kbps) ) + ( sum of delay (tens of µs) ) ]
bandwidth takes the MINIMUM along the path · delay takes the SUM
WIDE METRICS
64-bit with a larger scale factor, needed once links exceed
10 Gbps — the classic 32-bit value saturates and ties.
A PATH THAT LOOKS FAST AND SCORES SLOW
R1
R2
R3
R4
R5
last hop 100G
Delay is tiny and the hop count is small, so this looks like the best path.
But the minimum bandwidth is 100 Mbps, so the whole path is scored as 100 Mbps.
The comparison that surprises people
Path A: 4 hops, 100G / 100G / 100M / 100G
Path B: 3 hops, 1G / 1G / 1G
EIGRP prefers path B: A is capped at 100 Mbps.
In reality A is about 1000× faster for bulk flow, but the
composite metric cannot express that — by design.
WHAT TO DO ABOUT IT
1. Do not use a composite metric as a proxy for capacity. It answers “which path is less constrained”, not “which path has more room right now”.
2. Tune delay when the intent is path preference. Delay sums, so it behaves like an additive cost and is the honest knob.
3. Use wide metrics above 10 Gbps, or the value saturates and distinct paths start comparing equal.
The consequence for a mixed-bandwidth network: the composite metric is dominated by the slowest link, so a single 100 Mbps WAN hop
makes an otherwise 100G path unattractive. If the business intent is “prefer the fast path”, the metric cannot express it, and the design needs
an explicit policy layer (delay tuning, offset lists, or route-map based preference) rather than a hope that the formula will do it.
